text: There is a specific kind of madness that does not announce itself.
One day you are fine, the next someone's laugh is living rent-free in your head.
Your morning coffee tastes different and the part of your brain that's supposed to run the show has quietly handed over the keys.
The trouble isn't the feeling, it's what comes after.
When you realize you have been running on a hangover that you did not consent to and it refuses to live.
Love has taken away all my senses, like that of alcohol, effects of booze reside for a short period.
But your intoxication doesn't want to go away.
My heart keeps enjoying the hangover you created, your twinkling eyes, your enlightening smile, your ebony hair,
has stuck with me, like a newborn sticks to her mother.
My mind finds no way to get around you and it keeps coming back, like a moth attracted to the flame,
like waves to the shore, like coal to the winter, like a rainbow after the rain.
I know this isn't going to do any good to me, but the heart wants what the heart wants.
Earlier, my mind and heart worked in sync, but it seems like their ecosystems have collided,
deciding not to comply with each other, leaving me without a ground to stand on, or a sky to cover my head with.

The hangover metaphor works because hangovers have an end point.
You sleep it off, you hydrate, you move on.
This one doesn't schedule a time out.
And what keeps it alive isn't a vague ache, it's detail, twinkling eyes, an enlightening smile ebony hair.
The poem doesn't soften into abstraction, it stays specific, that's what makes it land,
vague longing forgettable, but a face, a real life, the particular features that stays,
that's a person and the poem makes no attempt to unite it into something specific,
and the poem makes no attempt to universalize it into something prettier.
These particular things are stuck, and I can't unstick them.
Then the moth to flame arrives, and it's not romantic.
Moths don't choose the flame, they are wired to the light.
No deliberation, no weighing of outcomes, just pull pure and indifferent to consequence.
When love starts feeling like physics instead of a decision, you are somewhere in you.
And the unsettling part isn't losing control, and discovering that you are not entirely unhappy about it.
There was one night while training and debugging a model pipeline for me.
Four terminals open, Databricks logs scrolling endlessly, coffee cold for an hour,
when our voice cut through the noise without warning.
Not the serious conversation, not the emotional moment, just the way she laughed,
after interrupting herself mid-sentence, days earlier.
And suddenly the entire debugging session disappeared behind that one tiny memory.
That's the unsettling thing about attachment.
The brain doesn't archive what matters logically.
It preserves texture, tone, timing.
The microscopic human details you never consciously choose to keep.
The point's real subject arrives near the end.
Their ecosystems have collided.
Earlier, mind and heart worked in sync.
That's the quiet operating system most of us rely on.
Desire checked by reason, want to wait against what makes sense orderly, predictable, safe.
Then someone walks in, and the whole architecture resets.
No ground to stand on, no sky to cover my head with.
That's not chaos, it's not obsession.
It's the sudden disorienting absence of coordinates.
The tools you've always used to navigate your own interior.
They no longer apply.
You're not broken.
You're standing at a false line where two tectonic plates have met.
And the ground that was always beneath you has dissolved mid-step.
I have had nights where one side of me was building airtight arguments for distance.
Rationalizing, analyzing patterns, trying to reduce emotion into something solvable like bad code.
And then another part of me would still reopen old messages.
Still search for meaning in silence.
Still stand emotionally in places.
My logic has already left hours earlier.
That's the collision the poem talks about.
Not heartbreak exactly.
People like realizing the mind and heart operate on completely different programming languages
when something or someone matters enough.
The poem doesn't resolve this.
It doesn't offer a path back to equilibrium.
It just tells the truth.
This is where you are now suspended, recalibrating without asking to.
The heart wants what the heart wants.
We say it like a disclaimer.
Half surrender, half of apology.
This poem says it differently.
Not as an excuse.
As a report from inside the collision, maybe when the mind and heart stop cooperating,
when you are left without ground or sky, that's not a malfunction.
That's a signal.
The only honest one you'll get that something actually matters enough to overturn the whole system.
No coordinates, no stability.
Just a full unfiltered weight of being alive enough to feel it.
That's not a problem to solve.
That's the experience itself.
This is breath of poetry.
If this poem reads something that you have been carrying quietly,
share it with the one person it makes you think of.
Or leave a line from it in the comments.
The one that stayed with you.
I will see you in the next one.
